beats.narration: Seven hundred and forty six drug shortage entries on the FDA list were updated in a single week. Which of them are on your hospital's shelf?
That is the daily job of a hospital pharmacy buyer. This is Shortage Radar, running right now, in real time, against the real FDA data.
beats.caption: A real run, live: no speed-up, no mock data

beats.narration: Before any model is involved, it has already read the FDA feed through Zetaris, replayed every saved snapshot in the World Model so it knows what changed, joined the hospital's stock with the FDA list in one query, and screened every third party field with the Scout guard.
beats.caption: Already done, no model involved: Zetaris query, World Model diff, stock join, Scout guard

beats.narration: Now Nemotron, through Nightshift, is choosing what to cover. This is the slow step, because it is the one place the model is allowed to think: choosing what matters is the judgement call. After that it writes one item at a time with thinking off, and a checker written in plain code verifies every claim, so a slow model cannot talk its way past it.

While that finishes, here is what is under the hood. Three Meterless engines do real work, and each passes its official test: World Model, eight of eight. H-MEM, thirteen of thirteen. Scout Intent, injection precision one point zero, recall point nine eight. The limits are on the page too: the hospital is fictional, Scout is pattern based, and the agent never predicts a shortage, because when we tested whether recalls predict them, the data said no.
beats.caption: Three Meterless engines, each passing the official tests, and the limits stated plainly

beats.narration: Six items need action today. Etomidate went from available to unavailable, with six days of stock left, and it names exactly what to buy instead: the same strength, from another manufacturer.
beats.caption: 6 to act on today  ·  13 FDA status changes, 8 on this hospital's shelf

beats.narration: Every line has a receipt. The drawer shows the swap options, and below that the evidence behind each sentence: the stock, the FDA status history from the World Model, and the Zetaris query with its SQL, one click away.
beats.caption: Every line has a receipt: the stock, the status history, and the SQL behind it

beats.narration: A swap has to be the same strength. A different concentration is a medication error, so on Morphine the other products are not offered as swaps. They go to a pharmacist for review, each with its reason.
beats.caption: Same strength only: everything else goes to pharmacist review, with the reason

beats.narration: When the buyer decides, H-MEM remembers. I record that I bought the alternate, and Etomidate moves to Handled. It stays out of tomorrow's brief until the FDA status changes again.
beats.caption: H-MEM remembers the decision: handled items stay out of the brief until the FDA status moves

beats.narration: Everything is logged. Each line names the agent, the Zetaris query, and the model that answered: Nemotron three point five Lightning, through Nightshift. The planner thinks, the writer doesn't, and the critic is code.
beats.caption: Every call is logged, with the model named: nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b

beats.narration: And anyone can run it with no keys at all. Sample mode replays a recorded live run, labelled as a replay, so a judge sees exactly what the live system produced.
beats.caption: No keys needed: Sample mode replays a recorded live run, labelled as a replay

beats.narration: Real data, real queries, real receipts. Shortage Radar doesn't guess what will run short. It tells you what to do about what just did.
